script.opening: "Thanks for seeing me. My periods stopped about six months ago, I did about ten pregnancy tests and they’re all negative — but now I’ve got actual milk leaking from my breasts, which is terrifying when you’re not pregnant. I googled it and I’m now convinced I’ve got a brain tumour. And honestly… the bit I keep coming back to is, does this mean I can’t have kids? That’s what’s really keeping me up."

facts.text: If explored: 6 months amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, reduced libido, with a markedly raised prolactin and negative pregnancy test — the classic hyperprolactinaemia syndrome. Headaches and possible visual-field disturbance ("bumping into door frames") raise the question of a pituitary macroadenoma pressing on the optic chiasm.

On direct questioning (easily missed): about 8 months ago — shortly before her periods stopped — she started a drug from a private clinic for anxiety/sleep — it turns out to be a dopamine-blocking agent (e.g. an antipsychotic such as a prescribed sulpiride/risperidone, or metoclopramide/domperidone) which RAISES prolactin. Drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia is common and reversible — a key alternative to a tumour that must be actively sought, and the dates fit. But a drug cause does not explain the headaches and "bumping into door frames", so pituitary imaging is still needed. (Also exclude hypothyroidism, renal impairment, pregnancy, macroprolactin, PCOS overlap.)

HIDDEN AGENDA — the stated worry is a brain tumour, but the deeper, less-voiced fear is FERTILITY: she and her partner had just started thinking about trying for a baby, and she’s terrified this means she’s "broken" and can never conceive. There’s also shame about the private "anxiety pills" she hasn’t told her partner or her GP about. Surfacing both is the consultation.

If reached: most hyperprolactinaemia (drug-induced, or a prolactinoma) is very treatable; prolactinomas usually respond well to medication (dopamine agonists), fertility is usually RECOVERABLE once prolactin is normalised — genuinely reassuring news once the cause is found.

Officially: to know it’s not a tumour and whether she can have children. What she needs: a structured work-up (repeat prolactin, exclude pregnancy/drugs/hypothyroidism, then pituitary MRI/endocrine referral, visual fields if symptoms), the drug cause actively sought, honest fertility reassurance, and the brain-tumour fear addressed.

ice.ideas: The milk and missed periods mean either pregnancy (ruled out) or a brain tumour.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — the deeper fear is fertility ("am I broken, can I never have kids?") just as she and her partner think about trying; plus shame about private "anxiety pills" she hasn’t disclosed.
ice.expectations: To be told it’s not a tumour and whether she can have children. What she actually needs: a structured cause work-up (incl. the drug cause), pituitary assessment, and honest, mostly-reassuring fertility information.

cues: Amenorrhoea + galactorrhoea + raised prolactin, pregnancy-negative — hyperprolactinaemia; find the cause, don’t jump to tumour.
Headaches + "bumping into door frames" — possible chiasmal compression (macroadenoma); ask visual fields.

Private "anxiety pills" started about 8 months ago, just before the periods stopped — the dopamine-blocker drug cause, easily missed (but it doesn’t explain the visual symptoms); and the unspoken fertility fear.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the hyperprolactinaemia syndrome (amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, reduced libido, raised prolactin, pregnancy-negative) and works it up STRUCTURED rather than jumping to "brain tumour" — confirms with a repeat prolactin on a rested sample (asking the lab about macroprolactin) and excludes the common reversible causes

Actively seeks the DRUG cause: asks specifically about all medicines incl. private/OTC, identifying the dopamine-blocking agent (antipsychotic/metoclopramide/domperidone) as a common, reversible cause — and also excludes pregnancy, primary hypothyroidism (TFTs) and renal cause

Screens for and acts on MACROADENOMA red flags: headache and visual-field disturbance (formal visual fields), and arranges PITUITARY MRI and endocrine referral, recognising chiasmal compression needs prompt assessment — and that a sudden severe headache with visual loss or eye-movement problems suggests pituitary apoplexy, an emergency (Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guidelines, 2011)

Gives honest, mostly-REASSURING fertility information: most hyperprolactinaemia is treatable (stop/switch the offending drug, or a dopamine agonist for a prolactinoma), and fertility usually recovers once prolactin normalises — directly addressing the deeper fear

Addresses the brain-tumour fear proportionately and the private-medication disclosure non-judgementally, advising on the offending drug (not stopping a needed psychiatric drug abruptly without a plan / liaise as appropriate)
Hears the stated tumour fear AND surfaces the deeper fertility fear, responding to both; handles the private "anxiety pills" shame without judgement so the drug history is complete
Balances honesty (a cause must be found, possible MRI) with genuine reassurance (highly treatable, fertility usually recoverable), pacing it to her anxiety

Safety-nets and follows up: repeat prolactin + TFTs + pregnancy test, MRI/endocrine referral and visual fields if symptoms, what to do if headache/vision worsens (urgent), the medication plan, and follow-up to go through results

worked.txt: "Let me explain what ties this together — the missed periods AND the milk. There’s a hormone called prolactin, the one that makes milk, and yours is high. When it’s up, it switches periods off and can cause milk even when you’re not pregnant. So this isn’t random or mysterious; it’s one hormone, and the job now is to find WHY it’s high — and most of the whys are very treatable."

"Before we think about anything in the head — can I ask about every tablet you take, including anything private or from the chemist? … The sleep/anxiety tablet from the clinic. That’s really important: some of those directly push prolactin up, and that’s a common, completely reversible cause. No judgement at all — I’m just glad to know, because it might be the whole answer."

"On the brain-tumour worry — high prolactin CAN come from a small, benign growth on the pituitary gland at the base of the brain, but ‘benign’ is the word, and even then it’s usually treated with tablets, not surgery. I do want a scan to look, and because you mentioned headaches and bumping into door frames, I’ll check your eyes’ side vision too — but the picture in your head is almost certainly worse than the reality."

"And the question that’s really keeping you up — can you have children. Here’s the honest, good news: this is one of the most fixable causes of periods stopping. Once we sort why the prolactin’s high — change the tablet, or treat a small growth — the prolactin comes down, your periods come back, and fertility usually returns with them. You are not broken."

"So: I’ll repeat the prolactin, check your thyroid and a pregnancy test, and arrange a scan of the pituitary and a check of your visual fields, plus refer you to the hormone specialists. We’ll work out the tablet situation safely — don’t stop the anxiety one suddenly; we’ll plan it. Bring your partner to the next appointment if it helps."

"If your headaches get much worse, or your vision changes — blurring, losing the edges, double vision — that’s urgent, contact us the same day; and a sudden, severe headache with loss of vision or double vision is an emergency — go to A&E or call 999 — because that’s the bit we don’t wait on. Otherwise, let’s get the tests done and I’ll go through everything with you. You came in fearing the worst on two fronts; the likely reality is a treatable hormone problem and a future that still very much includes children."

f.learning: The triad of amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and a markedly raised prolactin (pregnancy-negative) is hyperprolactinaemia — work it up structured rather than leaping to "brain tumour". Confirm with a repeat prolactin and exclude the common reversible causes: pregnancy, primary hypothyroidism, renal impairment, and especially DRUGS (dopamine-blockers — antipsychotics, metoclopramide, domperidone), which here is the easily-missed cause hiding in a private "anxiety pill" started shortly before her periods stopped — though it does not explain her visual symptoms. Screen for macroadenoma red flags (headache, visual-field loss from chiasmal compression) with formal visual fields, and arrange pituitary MRI and endocrine referral. The examinable hidden agenda is twofold: the stated brain-tumour fear, and the deeper, less-voiced FERTILITY fear ("am I broken?") as she and her partner consider trying — plus shame about undisclosed private medication. Deliver honest, mostly-reassuring information (hyperprolactinaemia is highly treatable; prolactinomas usually respond to dopamine agonists; fertility usually recovers once prolactin normalises), take a complete non-judgemental drug history, don’t stop a needed psychiatric drug abruptly, and safety-net visual symptoms as urgent.

knowledge.guideline: Endocrine Society hyperprolactinaemia guideline 2011 (international) · Pituitary Society consensus 2023 (international) · BNF
knowledge.summary: Amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and a raised prolactin with a negative pregnancy test is hyperprolactinaemia. Find the cause (drugs, thyroid, kidneys, pituitary) and act quickly on any visual symptoms.

points.t: Repeat the prolactin on a rested sample and ask the lab about macroprolactin, a harmless form that can make the result look high. Always exclude pregnancy first. There is no UK national guideline on hyperprolactinaemia; Endocrine Society 2011 (international) and Pituitary Society 2023 (international) guide the work-up.

points.h: Look for the common reversible causes
points.t: Dopamine-blocking drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, domperidone), primary hypothyroidism (check TSH), chronic kidney disease (check U&E) and pregnancy. Ask about every medicine, including private prescriptions and anything bought online or over the counter, and when each one was started.

A prolactinoma (micro- under 10 mm, macro- 10 mm or more), or any other pituitary mass pressing on the stalk, can raise prolactin. Headache and visual-field loss (classically bitemporal) suggest a macroadenoma pressing on the optic chiasm. Arrange pituitary MRI and endocrine referral.
A new visual-field defect needs same-day specialist or emergency assessment, with formal visual fields and urgent MRI.

Drug-induced: change or stop the drug only with the prescriber and a safe psychiatric plan; never stop abruptly. Prolactinoma: a dopamine agonist (cabergoline or bromocriptine; dose and monitoring per BNF) is first-line and usually normalises prolactin and shrinks the tumour. Periods and fertility usually return once prolactin falls.
Prolonged low oestrogen from hyperprolactinaemia affects bone health. This is another reason to find and treat the cause rather than watch.

dg.d: Open question first; let her tell the story of the missed periods, the milk and the negative tests before interpreting the result.
Partner and plans for a baby; anxiety and sleep that led her to a private clinic; what she has not yet told her partner.
Repeat prolactin (ask about macroprolactin), TSH, U&E, pregnancy test; formal visual fields; pituitary MRI through endocrinology.
Drug-induced (dopamine blocker) versus hypothyroidism, renal cause, prolactinoma or another pituitary mass; checks the drug timeline against the amenorrhoea.
Screened for mass effect (headache, visual-field loss) and knew sudden severe headache with visual loss is an emergency.
Named hyperprolactinaemia in plain language, with the drug and pituitary as the two main explanations to test.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Referral to endocrinology with MRI; urgent fields; liaised with the private prescriber rather than stopping the drug abruptly; honest fertility information.
Kept her anxiety and sleep covered in the medicine plan; considered the effect of low oestrogen on bone if prolonged.
Results appointment booked; same-day help for sudden headache or worsening vision; partner welcome at follow-up.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up the headaches, “bumping into door frames” and the hesitation about medicines, and explored each.
Idea (pregnancy or a brain tumour); concern (fertility — “am I broken?”); expectation (to hear it isn’t a tumour and whether she can have children).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — the deeper fear is fertility ("am I broken, can I never have kids?") just as she and her partner think about trying; plus shame about private "anxiety pills" she hasn’t disclosed — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Hannah, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for joining the video. I’ve got your blood results here, but before I say anything, tell me how things have been and what’s been on your mind.
model.why: Opens with her story before the numbers

model.text: My periods stopped six months ago. I’ve done about ten pregnancy tests, all negative, and now there’s actual milk coming from my breasts. I googled it and I’m convinced it’s a brain tumour. And the thing I keep coming back to is, does this mean I can’t have kids?

That’s a lot to be carrying, and I’m glad you said both things: the tumour worry and the question about children. I promise we’ll answer both today. Can I ask a few questions first, then explain what the result means and agree a plan?
model.why: Names both concerns and sets a clear agenda

model.text: Yes, please.
Apart from the periods and the milk, have you noticed anything else — changes in how you feel, your sex drive, your skin or weight?
model.why: Open screen for the hyperprolactinaemia picture

model.text: My libido’s gone, honestly. I thought that was just stress.
That fits with the result, so it’s useful. Any headaches?
A few, on and off. Nothing dramatic.
And your eyesight — any blurring, double vision, or bumping into things on one side?
Funny you say that. I keep catching my shoulder on door frames. I thought I was just clumsy.
I’m really glad you mentioned that. It might be nothing, but it can mean the edges of your vision aren’t picking things up, so I want your side vision tested properly and soon. I’ll come back to why.
model.why: Acts on the visual-field cue rather than passing over it

model.text: Now, this one really matters: can you tell me about every tablet or medicine you take — including anything from a private clinic, online, or the chemist? There’s no judgement at all; some medicines raise this hormone.
model.why: Non-judgemental, complete drug history including private supply

model.text: (pause) There is something. A private clinic gave me a tablet for anxiety and sleep. I haven’t told anyone — not even my partner.
Thank you for trusting me with that. It could be really important. Do you know what it’s called, and roughly when you started it?
model.why: Seeks the dopamine-blocker cause and its timing

model.text: I’d have to check the box. I started it fairly recently.

Could you read me the name or send a photo after this call? Some tablets used for anxiety and sleep block dopamine, and that pushes prolactin up. I’ll also want to line up when you started it with when your periods stopped, because if the periods went first, something else may be going on as well.
model.why: Explains the mechanism and checks the timeline fits

model.text: You said the children question is what keeps you up at night. Would you tell me a bit more?
model.why: Returns to the deeper, less-voiced fear

model.text: We’d just started talking about trying for a baby. And now I feel broken. I keep thinking I’ve ruined it.
That sounds really frightening, and it makes sense you’d feel that way. I can give you some genuinely good news on that in a moment. What were you hoping we’d do today?
Tell me it’s not a tumour. And whether I can still have children.

Here’s what ties it together. Prolactin is the hormone that makes breast milk. Yours is high, and when it’s high it switches periods off and can cause milk even when you’re not pregnant. So this is one hormone, and the job now is to find out why it’s high.
model.why: Names the syndrome in plain language

model.text: So it could just be the tablet?

It could be — that’s one of the commonest causes and it’s reversible. Other causes I’ll check are an underactive thyroid and the kidneys. The other possibility is a small growth on the pituitary gland at the base of the brain. If it is that, it’s almost always benign, and it’s usually treated with tablets, not surgery.
model.why: Structured differential; proportionate answer to the tumour fear

model.text: But you still want a scan.

Yes — because of the headaches and the door frames, I don’t want to guess. And about children: this is one of the most treatable reasons for periods stopping. Once the prolactin comes down — by changing a tablet or treating a small growth — periods usually come back, and fertility usually comes back with them. You are not broken.
(tearful) I really needed to hear that.

So here’s what I suggest. A repeat prolactin, a thyroid test, a kidney test and a fresh pregnancy test. An urgent check of your side vision with an optician or the eye clinic. And a referral to the hormone specialists, who will arrange an MRI scan of the pituitary. How does that sound?
Okay. And the anxiety tablet — should I just stop it?

Please don’t stop it suddenly. Once I know its name, I’ll speak to the clinic that prescribed it, and we’ll plan a safe switch if it’s the cause, so your anxiety and sleep are still looked after. Would you be happy for me to contact them?
model.why: Safe medicine plan with consent to share information

model.text: Yes, that’s fine. I think I need to tell my partner too.
That’s your choice, and you’re welcome to bring your partner to the results appointment if it would help.

One important thing. If you get a sudden, severe headache, or your vision gets worse — blurring, losing the edges, or double vision — that needs same-day help: contact us straight away, or go to A&E if we’re closed. I’ll see you again as soon as the blood results are back. Can you tell me in your own words what we’ve agreed?
Bloods, eye test, hormone specialist and a scan. Don’t stop the tablet, send you the name. And it’s very likely fixable, including having a baby.
That’s exactly it. You came in fearing the worst on two fronts — the likely answer is a treatable hormone problem. Anything else before we finish?
model.why: Summarises and checks for anything unaddressed

model.text: No. Thank you — that’s a huge weight off.

social.t: She and her partner had just started talking about trying for a baby. The fertility fear is the real agenda; answer it clearly.
Private treatment for anxiety and sleep, kept from her partner and the practice. Shame blocks disclosure, so a non-judgemental tone is what gets the full history.

legal.t: Whether she tells her partner is her decision. Contacting the private prescriber needs her consent, which she gives; record it.
If formal testing confirms a visual-field defect and she drives, she must meet the DVLA visual-field standard and may need to notify the DVLA. Advise her once the result is known.

professional.t: GMC guidance on prescribing (2021) expects prescribers to share information with the patient’s GP. Where that hasn’t happened, liaise with the private clinic, with consent, before changing the medicine.
Explain that a pituitary cause must be looked for, and put it in proportion. Don’t promise it isn’t a growth, and don’t lead with “tumour”.

community.t: The Pituitary Foundation (information and helpline) if a pituitary cause is confirmed; NHS Talking Therapies for anxiety as an alternative or addition to medication.

redFlags: Visual-field loss (“bumping into door frames”), blurring or double vision — possible chiasmal compression
Sudden severe headache with visual loss or eye-movement problems — possible pituitary apoplexy, an emergency
Symptoms of other pituitary hormone deficiency (profound fatigue, dizziness, cold intolerance)
psychosocial: Plans for a baby with her partner, and fear that she is “broken”
Anxiety and poor sleep that led to a private clinic; secrecy and shame about the tablet
Impact of the brain-tumour search on her mood and sleep
ice: Idea: “It’s either pregnancy — which it isn’t — or a brain tumour”
Concern: “Does this mean I can’t have kids?”
Expectation: to be told it’s not a tumour, and whether she can still have children

playbook.diagnosis: Hyperprolactinaemia with a negative pregnancy test, most likely caused by the dopamine-blocking private medicine or a pituitary lesion. Visual symptoms mean a macroadenoma must be checked for urgently.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Prolactin is the hormone that makes breast milk. Yours is high, and that switches your periods off and causes the milk. It’s like one switch stuck on. Our job is to find what’s holding it on — a tablet, the thyroid, or a small, almost always benign growth on a gland at the base of the brain.”

management.reflectIce: “You came in worried about a tumour, but the question keeping you up is children. The honest answer is good news: once we bring the prolactin down, periods and fertility usually come back.”
management.psychosocial: Keep the drug history non-judgemental; plan a safe change to the anxiety medicine with the private prescriber so her anxiety and sleep are still treated; leave the decision to tell her partner with her.
sharedPlan: Repeat prolactin (with macroprolactin), TSH, U&E and pregnancy test
Urgent formal visual-field test; endocrine referral with pituitary MRI
Identify the private tablet and liaise with the prescriber about a safe switch; don’t stop it abruptly
safetyNet: Sudden severe headache or worsening vision (blurring, loss of side vision, double vision) — same-day help
Results appointment booked; partner welcome; fertility discussed again once the cause is known

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed less on endocrinology than on sequencing: jumping to “tumour”, missing the private tablet, and leaving the fertility question unanswered. Each pattern below is common and fixable.

items.fail: Asking “Are you on any medication?”, hearing “no”, and moving on.
items.why: She has no repeat medicines on record, and the private anxiety tablet is the most likely reversible cause. A closed question misses it.
items.fix: Ask specifically: “Anything from a private clinic, online, or the chemist — even for sleep?” Then ask when it started and check that against when the periods stopped.

items.fail: Treating “bumping into door frames” as clumsiness and arranging a routine referral only.
items.why: Possible visual-field loss suggests chiasmal compression, so the speed of the work-up has to change.
items.fix: Arrange urgent formal visual fields, refer to endocrinology for MRI, and safety-net sudden headache with visual loss as an emergency.

items.fail: Answering the tumour question in detail and never getting to fertility.
items.why: She says fertility is what keeps her up at night. Missing the less-voiced concern is the classic Relating fail.
items.fix: Name both at the start and give the fertility answer plainly: periods and fertility usually return once prolactin normalises.

items.fail: Reacting to the private tablet with “You shouldn’t get medicines like that privately.”
items.why: Shame is why she hid it. A judgemental response closes the history and damages trust.
items.fix: “Thank you for telling me — that might be the whole answer.” Then ask her consent to contact the prescriber.

items.fail: Jargon: “You’ve got hyperprolactinaemia, probably a microadenoma, we’ll do an MRI and check for macroprolactin.”
items.why: Language the patient can’t follow is flagged as poor Global Skills, and “adenoma” sounds like cancer to her.
items.fix: “One hormone is high; it switches periods off and makes milk. We’ll find what’s holding the switch on.”

items.fail: Telling her to stop the tablet today, or ending without a plan for it.
items.why: Stopping a psychiatric drug abruptly is unsafe, and an unmanaged anxiety relapse is a foreseeable harm.
items.fix: “Don’t stop it suddenly. Send me the name, I’ll speak to the clinic, and we’ll switch safely so your anxiety and sleep are still covered.”

timeMap.d: She opens with milk, negative tests, a brain-tumour fear and “can I have kids?”. Let her finish and name both worries back.
Libido, headache, visual fields (“door frames”). Ask about EVERY medicine including private supply — and when it started.
Reach the fertility fear and the undisclosed tablet. Stay non-judgemental so the drug history is complete.
One hormone, several causes. Bloods, urgent visual fields, endocrine referral with MRI. Fertility usually recovers. Don’t stop the tablet suddenly.
Sudden severe headache or worsening vision = same-day help. Results appointment. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Jumps to “we need to rule out a brain tumour” without asking about medicines; never finds the private tablet; misses the door-frame cue; leaves the fertility question unanswered; or tells her to stop the tablet today.
wordPics.pass: Explains hyperprolactinaemia plainly; takes a full drug history and finds the private tablet; checks TSH, U&E and a repeat prolactin; refers for MRI and endocrinology; addresses fertility; gives a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: acts on the visual-field cue with urgent formal fields; checks the drug timeline against the amenorrhoea; plans a safe switch with the prescriber and her consent; gives clear, warm fertility reassurance tied to her words (“you are not broken”); teach-back and a specific apoplexy safety-net.

avoid.dont: “It could be a tumour, so we need a brain scan.”
avoid.instead: “This is one hormone that’s high, and the common causes — including a tablet — are very treatable. A scan is part of checking properly.”
avoid.why: Leading with “tumour” confirms her worst fear before you’ve found the cause.

avoid.dont: “Just stop the anxiety tablet and we’ll recheck.”
avoid.instead: “Please don’t stop it suddenly — let me speak to the clinic and plan a safe switch.”
avoid.why: Abruptly stopping a psychiatric drug is unsafe, and the prescriber needs to be involved.

avoid.dont: “Let’s not worry about fertility until we know more.”
avoid.instead: “Here’s the honest good news: once prolactin comes down, periods and fertility usually come back.”
avoid.why: Deferring her real question loses the Relating marks and leaves her fear untouched.

SCA_MODELS.text: Now, this one really matters: can you tell me about every tablet or medicine you take — including anything from a private clinic, online, or the chemist? There’s no judgement at all; some medicines raise this hormone.
SCA_MODELS.why: Non-judgemental, complete drug history including private supply

SCA_MODELS.text: (pause) There is something. A private clinic gave me a tablet for anxiety and sleep. I haven’t told anyone — not even my partner.
Thank you for trusting me with that. It could be really important. Do you know what it’s called, and roughly when you started it?
SCA_MODELS.why: Seeks the dopamine-blocker cause and its timing

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d have to check the box. I started it fairly recently.

Could you read me the name or send a photo after this call? Some tablets used for anxiety and sleep block dopamine, and that pushes prolactin up. I’ll also want to line up when you started it with when your periods stopped, because if the periods went first, something else may be going on as well.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains the mechanism and checks the timeline fits

SCA_MODELS.text: You said the children question is what keeps you up at night. Would you tell me a bit more?
SCA_MODELS.why: Returns to the deeper, less-voiced fear

SCA_MODELS.text: We’d just started talking about trying for a baby. And now I feel broken. I keep thinking I’ve ruined it.
That sounds really frightening, and it makes sense you’d feel that way. I can give you some genuinely good news on that in a moment. What were you hoping we’d do today?
Tell me it’s not a tumour. And whether I can still have children.

Here’s what ties it together. Prolactin is the hormone that makes breast milk. Yours is high, and when it’s high it switches periods off and can cause milk even when you’re not pregnant. So this is one hormone, and the job now is to find out why it’s high.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the syndrome in plain language

SCA_MODELS.text: So it could just be the tablet?

It could be — that’s one of the commonest causes and it’s reversible. Other causes I’ll check are an underactive thyroid and the kidneys. The other possibility is a small growth on the pituitary gland at the base of the brain. If it is that, it’s almost always benign, and it’s usually treated with tablets, not surgery.
SCA_MODELS.why: Structured differential; proportionate answer to the tumour fear

SCA_MODELS.text: But you still want a scan.

Yes — because of the headaches and the door frames, I don’t want to guess. And about children: this is one of the most treatable reasons for periods stopping. Once the prolactin comes down — by changing a tablet or treating a small growth — periods usually come back, and fertility usually comes back with them. You are not broken.
(tearful) I really needed to hear that.

So here’s what I suggest. A repeat prolactin, a thyroid test, a kidney test and a fresh pregnancy test. An urgent check of your side vision with an optician or the eye clinic. And a referral to the hormone specialists, who will arrange an MRI scan of the pituitary. How does that sound?
Okay. And the anxiety tablet — should I just stop it?

Please don’t stop it suddenly. Once I know its name, I’ll speak to the clinic that prescribed it, and we’ll plan a safe switch if it’s the cause, so your anxiety and sleep are still looked after. Would you be happy for me to contact them?
SCA_MODELS.why: Safe medicine plan with consent to share information

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes, that’s fine. I think I need to tell my partner too.
That’s your choice, and you’re welcome to bring your partner to the results appointment if it would help.

One important thing. If you get a sudden, severe headache, or your vision gets worse — blurring, losing the edges, or double vision — that needs same-day help: contact us straight away, or go to A&E if we’re closed. I’ll see you again as soon as the blood results are back. Can you tell me in your own words what we’ve agreed?
Bloods, eye test, hormone specialist and a scan. Don’t stop the tablet, send you the name. And it’s very likely fixable, including having a baby.
That’s exactly it. You came in fearing the worst on two fronts — the likely answer is a treatable hormone problem. Anything else before we finish?
SCA_MODELS.why: Summarises and checks for anything unaddressed

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Thank you — that’s a huge weight off.

SCA_STEM.name: Hannah Reid
pmh: Six months of absent periods — bloods arranged at a previous appointment
meds: No regular medication on the practice record
SCA_STEM.recent: Bloods for amenorrhoea: prolactin about 2200 mU/L (lab upper limit about 500). Pregnancy test negative. No TSH, renal function or repeat prolactin yet on file.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation to discuss her blood results.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: Endocrine Society hyperprolactinaemia guideline 2011 (international) · Pituitary Society consensus 2023 (international) · BNF
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and a raised prolactin with a negative pregnancy test is hyperprolactinaemia. Find the cause (drugs, thyroid, kidneys, pituitary) and act quickly on any visual symptoms.

points.t: Repeat the prolactin on a rested sample and ask the lab about macroprolactin, a harmless form that can make the result look high. Always exclude pregnancy first. There is no UK national guideline on hyperprolactinaemia; Endocrine Society 2011 (international) and Pituitary Society 2023 (international) guide the work-up.

points.h: Look for the common reversible causes
points.t: Dopamine-blocking drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, domperidone), primary hypothyroidism (check TSH), chronic kidney disease (check U&E) and pregnancy. Ask about every medicine, including private prescriptions and anything bought online or over the counter, and when each one was started.

A prolactinoma (micro- under 10 mm, macro- 10 mm or more), or any other pituitary mass pressing on the stalk, can raise prolactin. Headache and visual-field loss (classically bitemporal) suggest a macroadenoma pressing on the optic chiasm. Arrange pituitary MRI and endocrine referral.
A new visual-field defect needs same-day specialist or emergency assessment, with formal visual fields and urgent MRI.

Drug-induced: change or stop the drug only with the prescriber and a safe psychiatric plan; never stop abruptly. Prolactinoma: a dopamine agonist (cabergoline or bromocriptine; dose and monitoring per BNF) is first-line and usually normalises prolactin and shrinks the tumour. Periods and fertility usually return once prolactin falls.
Prolonged low oestrogen from hyperprolactinaemia affects bone health. This is another reason to find and treat the cause rather than watch.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question first; let her tell the story of the missed periods, the milk and the negative tests before interpreting the result.
Partner and plans for a baby; anxiety and sleep that led her to a private clinic; what she has not yet told her partner.
Picked up the headaches, “bumping into door frames” and the hesitation about medicines, and explored each.
Idea (pregnancy or a brain tumour); concern (fertility — “am I broken?”); expectation (to hear it isn’t a tumour and whether she can have children).
Repeat prolactin (ask about macroprolactin), TSH, U&E, pregnancy test; formal visual fields; pituitary MRI through endocrinology.
Drug-induced (dopamine blocker) versus hypothyroidism, renal cause, prolactinoma or another pituitary mass; checks the drug timeline against the amenorrhoea.
Screened for mass effect (headache, visual-field loss) and knew sudden severe headache with visual loss is an emergency.
Named hyperprolactinaemia in plain language, with the drug and pituitary as the two main explanations to test.
Referral to endocrinology with MRI; urgent fields; liaised with the private prescriber rather than stopping the drug abruptly; honest fertility information.
Kept her anxiety and sleep covered in the medicine plan; considered the effect of low oestrogen on bone if prolonged.
Results appointment booked; same-day help for sudden headache or worsening vision; partner welcome at follow-up.

social.t: She and her partner had just started talking about trying for a baby. The fertility fear is the real agenda; answer it clearly.
Private treatment for anxiety and sleep, kept from her partner and the practice. Shame blocks disclosure, so a non-judgemental tone is what gets the full history.

legal.t: Whether she tells her partner is her decision. Contacting the private prescriber needs her consent, which she gives; record it.
If formal testing confirms a visual-field defect and she drives, she must meet the DVLA visual-field standard and may need to notify the DVLA. Advise her once the result is known.

professional.t: GMC guidance on prescribing (2021) expects prescribers to share information with the patient’s GP. Where that hasn’t happened, liaise with the private clinic, with consent, before changing the medicine.
Explain that a pituitary cause must be looked for, and put it in proportion. Don’t promise it isn’t a growth, and don’t lead with “tumour”.

community.t: The Pituitary Foundation (information and helpline) if a pituitary cause is confirmed; NHS Talking Therapies for anxiety as an alternative or addition to medication.

redFlags: Visual-field loss (“bumping into door frames”), blurring or double vision — possible chiasmal compression
Sudden severe headache with visual loss or eye-movement problems — possible pituitary apoplexy, an emergency
Symptoms of other pituitary hormone deficiency (profound fatigue, dizziness, cold intolerance)
psychosocial: Plans for a baby with her partner, and fear that she is “broken”
Anxiety and poor sleep that led to a private clinic; secrecy and shame about the tablet
Impact of the brain-tumour search on her mood and sleep
ice: Idea: “It’s either pregnancy — which it isn’t — or a brain tumour”
Concern: “Does this mean I can’t have kids?”
Expectation: to be told it’s not a tumour, and whether she can still have children

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Hyperprolactinaemia with a negative pregnancy test, most likely caused by the dopamine-blocking private medicine or a pituitary lesion. Visual symptoms mean a macroadenoma must be checked for urgently.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Prolactin is the hormone that makes breast milk. Yours is high, and that switches your periods off and causes the milk. It’s like one switch stuck on. Our job is to find what’s holding it on — a tablet, the thyroid, or a small, almost always benign growth on a gland at the base of the brain.”

management.reflectIce: “You came in worried about a tumour, but the question keeping you up is children. The honest answer is good news: once we bring the prolactin down, periods and fertility usually come back.”
management.psychosocial: Keep the drug history non-judgemental; plan a safe change to the anxiety medicine with the private prescriber so her anxiety and sleep are still treated; leave the decision to tell her partner with her.
sharedPlan: Repeat prolactin (with macroprolactin), TSH, U&E and pregnancy test
Urgent formal visual-field test; endocrine referral with pituitary MRI
Identify the private tablet and liaise with the prescriber about a safe switch; don’t stop it abruptly
safetyNet: Sudden severe headache or worsening vision (blurring, loss of side vision, double vision) — same-day help
Results appointment booked; partner welcome; fertility discussed again once the cause is known

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed less on endocrinology than on sequencing: jumping to “tumour”, missing the private tablet, and leaving the fertility question unanswered. Each pattern below is common and fixable.

items.fail: Asking “Are you on any medication?”, hearing “no”, and moving on.
items.why: She has no repeat medicines on record, and the private anxiety tablet is the most likely reversible cause. A closed question misses it.
items.fix: Ask specifically: “Anything from a private clinic, online, or the chemist — even for sleep?” Then ask when it started and check that against when the periods stopped.

items.fail: Treating “bumping into door frames” as clumsiness and arranging a routine referral only.
items.why: Possible visual-field loss suggests chiasmal compression, so the speed of the work-up has to change.
items.fix: Arrange urgent formal visual fields, refer to endocrinology for MRI, and safety-net sudden headache with visual loss as an emergency.

items.fail: Answering the tumour question in detail and never getting to fertility.
items.why: She says fertility is what keeps her up at night. Missing the less-voiced concern is the classic Relating fail.
items.fix: Name both at the start and give the fertility answer plainly: periods and fertility usually return once prolactin normalises.

items.fail: Reacting to the private tablet with “You shouldn’t get medicines like that privately.”
items.why: Shame is why she hid it. A judgemental response closes the history and damages trust.
items.fix: “Thank you for telling me — that might be the whole answer.” Then ask her consent to contact the prescriber.

items.fail: Jargon: “You’ve got hyperprolactinaemia, probably a microadenoma, we’ll do an MRI and check for macroprolactin.”
items.why: Language the patient can’t follow is flagged as poor Global Skills, and “adenoma” sounds like cancer to her.
items.fix: “One hormone is high; it switches periods off and makes milk. We’ll find what’s holding the switch on.”

items.fail: Telling her to stop the tablet today, or ending without a plan for it.
items.why: Stopping a psychiatric drug abruptly is unsafe, and an unmanaged anxiety relapse is a foreseeable harm.
items.fix: “Don’t stop it suddenly. Send me the name, I’ll speak to the clinic, and we’ll switch safely so your anxiety and sleep are still covered.”
